author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have learned with pain that our troops allowed themselves to be surprised yesterday at the village of St. Michel. […] You must not be astonished, my dear general, at the little check you have received; it will only be the prelude to our victory. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Eve of Montenotte: a check at San Michele, answered with a promise of revenge. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have transferred my head-quarters to Albenga. The movement which I found commenced against Genoa has drawn the enemy out of his winter quarters. Beaulieu has published a manifesto, to which I shall reply after the battle. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Headquarters moved up; Genoa's alarm spoiled his plan to catch Beaulieu napping. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Italian campaign has commenced. I have forwarded a report on the battle of Montenotte. After manoeuvring for three days in order to conceal his intentions, Beaulieu attacked the right of our army with 10,000 men. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: First victory dispatch: Montenotte, three days of manoeuvre. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will find the details of the battles of Montenotte and Millesimo in the report forwarded to the Directory. I cannot conceal from you that I am seconded neither by the artillery nor the engineers, as, in spite of your orders, I have not a single one of the officers I asked for. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Dateline partly illegible in scan; placed by content after Montenotte–Millesimo. Fighting Paris as well as Piedmont: no engineers, no artillery officers sent. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The soldier without bread is driven to commit acts which make one blush to be a man. […] I have 100,000 men against me, and can oppose only 34,000 infantry and 3,500 cavalry to that force. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Dateline partly illegible in scan; placed by content after Mondovi. Mondovi report: the army he found — without bread, without discipline — and made examples. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “. Everything is going on well. There is not so much pillaging. The first thirst of an army in want of everything has been quenched. There was an excuse for these unfortunate fellows who after having sighed for three years on the summit of the Alps, reached the promised land and desired to enjoy it. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Pillage punished: three shot, hard labour. Order before politics. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The village of Coni has been occupied by our troops. I feel sure that you will approve of the suspension of arms granted to the Sardinians; it is an armistice accorded to one wing of an army, giving me time to beat the other. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Sardinia's armistice — signed against the Directory's orders: a king at his discretion. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We reached Acqui yesterday. Beaulieu flies so fast that we cannot catch him Send me a geographical, historical, political, and topographical note on the imperial fiefs in the neighbourhood of Genoa; also a note on the Dukes of Parma, Placentia, and Modena; the forces they have in the field; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Connoisseur's shopping list: notes on fiefs, dukes — and their pictures and statues. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your answer. I beg you will express to the Corps Legislatif the thanks of the army for the honourable decree which it has voted; it is the most grateful recompense that the army can receive. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Thanks of the army voted; devotion to the constitution professed — for now. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We have at last crossed the Po. The second campaign has commenced. Beaulieu is disconcerted; he miscalculates, and continually falls into the snares I set for him. Perhaps he wishes to give battle, for he has both audacity and energy, but not genius. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Dateline partly illegible in scan; placed by content at the Po crossing. 'We have at last crossed the Po': the second campaign opens; Beaulieu wants genius. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The army of Italy is in the greatest distress It is every day reinforcedy and its necessities increase in proportion. When the Directory gave me the command of this army it drew up a plan of offensive warfare necessitating prompt measures and extraordinary resources. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: An army in distress: pay months late, needs growing with every recruit. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The nobles, priests, and agents of Austria lead the people of these splendid countries astray. The French army, as generous as it is strong, will treat all peaceful inhabitants with fraternity; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Dateline partly illegible in scan; placed by content amid the Milan proclamations. Proclamation: fraternity for the peaceful — fire from heaven for rebels. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It is to deliver the finest country of Europe from the iron yoke of the arrogant house of Austria that the French army has braved the most difficult obstacles. Victory, in harmony with justice, has crowned these efforts. The remains of the enemy's army have fallen back behind the Mincio. […]”
sourceTitle: To the Republic of Venice, *' Brescia, 1796-05-29
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Entering Venetian land in pursuit — but remembering long friendship. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Soldiers, — You dashed like a torrent from the summit of the Apennines; you have overthrown, dispersed, and scattered all who opposed your march. " Piedmont, delivered from Austrian tyranny, has given vent to her natural sentiments of peace and friendship towards France. […]”
sourceTitle: To his brothers in arms, Milan, 1796-05-20
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: 'Milan is ours': the torrent from the Apennines proclaimed to the troops. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “. Commissioner Salicetti will forward you a list of the contributions we have imposed. You can at present count upon from 6,000,000 to 8,000,000 francs in gold or silver, ingots, or jewels which are at your disposal at Genoa at the house of one of the first bankers. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: War pays: 6–8 millions in gold, ingots and jewels at Genoa for Paris. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “General Augereau's division passed the Po yesterday and arrived at Bologna on the 19th; he found 400 soldiers of the Pope there and made them prisoners. […] We have captured the Cardinal Legate, all the officers of the staff, and taken four flags; also the Cardinal Legate of Ferrara, together with the commandant of that fort, who is a knight of Malta. […] Monge, Berthollet, and Thouin are at Pavia, where they are busy enriching our Jardin des Plantes and cabinet of natural history. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Augereau's victory brought papal prisoners, both legates and four flags; Monge, Berthollet and Thouin are at Pavia. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The siege of Mantua, sir, is more disastrous for humanity than two campaigns. Brave men ought to affront danger, but not the pestilence of a marsh. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Chivalry to the enemy: Mantua's marshes kill more surely than battles. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Majesty, Europe desires peace. This disastrous war has lasted too long. I have the honour to notify to your Majesty that if you do not send plenipotentiaries to Paris to offer negotiations for peace, the Directory has ordered me to fill up the port of Trieste, […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: A 27-year-old to an emperor: send plenipotentiaries — or lose Trieste. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The army of General Alvinzi is on the Brenta and in the Tyrol, and that of the Republic along the Adige Mantua is invested with the greatest care You will see by the Emperor's letter that Wurmser must be in extrernis The army returns which you have sent are full of errors The army of Italy, […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Alvinzi on the Brenta; Wurmser in extremis; an army of 38,500 that should be 51,000. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Committee of Savants has reaped a good harvest at Ravenna, Rimini, Pesaro, Ancona, Loretto, and Perugia which will be at once forwarded to Paris. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Tolentino: the Pope pays for peace. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I send you by General Leclerc some interesting despatches concerning the situation of the army and the negotiations which have been commenced. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Preliminaries signed: Austria will treat without England. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will find inclosed the ratification of the Emperor to the preliminary treaty. The plenipotentiary of the Emperor regretted that the treaty had not been drawn up on parchment and that the seals were not larger. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Venice judged: an armed republic that plotted with Naples and the Pope. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Soldiers — To-day is the anniversary of the 14th July. You see before you the names of your comrades who have fallen on the field of honour for the liberty of the country; they have furnished you with a brilliant example. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Festival order of the day: the fallen as example. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter. The music for which you ask is being copied in the various towns of Italy. I shall take the greatest care to enrich the conservatory. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: The general with no soul for music writes to its inspectors. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Attempts have been made to disturb your Royal Highness, and to invent motives for dispute between you and the French Republic. " I consider it my duty to inform your Royal Highness 77 that the Directory having every reason to be satisfied with the conduct of your Royal Highness during the whole of t […]”
sourceTitle: To the Grand Duke of Tuscany, Milan, 1797-08-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Tuscany settled from Milan. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “To-day we proceeded to exchange the ratifications of the treaty of Campo Formio. All the members of the Congress have arrived and have paid me a visit. The King of Sweden has sent the Baron de Fersen as his ambassador. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: From Rastatt: peacemaking as power politics. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “. I know of nothing more respectable and worthy of the veneration of men than a priest who, imbued with the true spirit of the Gospel, is persuaded that he is in duty bound to obey the temporal power, and to maintain peace, tranquillity, and union in his diocese, &c.”
sourceTitle: To the Bishop of Malta, *'Cn Board the "Orient/ iitk, 1798-06-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: To Malta's bishop, days before the island falls. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We have at Cairo, Citizen General, a very fine mint. We require all the ingots which we left at Alexandria, in exchange for the coin given to us by the merchants. I beg you will therefore assemble the merchants to whom the said ingots were given, and ask to have them back. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Written the day of the Pyramids. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “A Portuguese squadron composed of four vessels of war and two frigates arrived before Alexandria on the 29th August, and joined the squadron of cruisers left behind by the English. Render us justice, Citizen Director, for this impertinence on the part of the Queen of Portugal. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Two months in: accounting to Paris. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Perverse men led some of you astray; they have perished. God has ordered me to be clement and merciful to the people; I have been clement and merciful towards you. " I was angry with you for revolting. During two months 1 deprived you of your divan; but to-day I restore it. […]”
sourceTitle: To the inhabitants of Cairo, Cairo, 1798-12-21
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Proclamation after the Cairo revolt. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Order Citizen Deriot to march with twenty-five troopers, at 2 A.M., to fort Sulkowski, to pick up thirty men of the 22nd in garrison there, and with this force to enter the village of El Matarzeh, where it is indispensable he should arrive an hour before daybreak, in order to kill some Arabs. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Night orders: troopers at 2 a.m., Arabs at dawn. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You have already been informed of my arrival on the shores of the Red Sea, with a numerous and invincible army, animated with the desire of delivering you from the iron yoke of England. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: To Mysore: the eastern alliance against England that never was. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The General-in-Chief Bonaparte commanding the armies of the French Republic begs me to inform you that in virtue of the cartel of exchange between the two nations, he sends you the English prisoners captured at Hayfa, &c., &c. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Headquarters cartel letter to his Acre adversary. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “There is no other God but God, and Mohammed is His prophet! *' To the Divan of Cairo, chosen among the wisest, the most educated, and the most enlightened persons. May the grace of the Prophet be on you! " I write you this to inform you that. […]”
sourceTitle: To the Divan of Cairo, Cairo, 1799-07-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Governing Egypt through its notables. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have not been well satisfied, Citizen General, with your operations during the movements which have just taken place. No matter what events arise, nothing should hinder a soldier from obeying orders; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Upper Egypt orders, weeks before the secret departure. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will find inclosed, Citizen General, an order to take over the command in chief of the army. The fear of the English cruisers returning makes me hasten my departure. I take with me Berthier, Lannes, Murat, Andreossy, and Marmont, the citizens Monge and Berthollet. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: The farewell: Egypt to Kléber; France the prize. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Citizen Directors, — Since I left France I have received only one of your despatches, which reached me when I was before Acre. It contained the news of our successes at Naples, which made me conjecture an approaching war on the Continent. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Back in France, reporting to the Directory he will overthrow in weeks. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have just received your letter of the 22nd Floreal. I beg you will have the inclosed printed at length in the official journal, for it is well for the public to know the situation of the army of Egypt when I left it, and how exaggerated are the reports made by the agents of England. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Second Italian campaign opens: First Consul writing to his colleagues. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Write to General Kleber that when the news of the capitulation arrived, the Brest squadron was about to sail with 4,000 troops and war stores; that we have only just learned the capitulation has been broken, and that he has reconquered Egypt; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: After Marengo: Kléber, Egypt, and broken capitulations. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I beg you will invite two of the best virtuosos to go to Paris in order to sing a duo in Italian at the fete of the 14th July. You will give them all that is necessary for their voyage, &c. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Virtuosos for the national fête — war administration as usual. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Horatio Nelson
displayText: “I always was of opinion; have ever acted up to it, and never had any reason to repent it, that one Englishman was equal to three Frenchmen: had this been an English town I am sure it would not have been taken by them." In his journal of 23rd May he wrote: […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. I — prints Nelson's letters as context — public domain
context: OPPOSING VOICE: Nelson besieging Calvi — George III, King of Corsica. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Horatio Nelson
displayText: “. We have now done with Corsica; I have seen the first and the last of that kingdom. Its situation certainly was most desirable for us, but the generality of its inhabitants are so greedy of wealth, and so jealous of each other, […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. I — prints Nelson's letters as context — public domain
context: OPPOSING VOICE: Nelson quits Corsica — 'the first and the last of that kingdom.' English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have beaten the enemy. Kilmaine will send you the account. I am dead of fatigue. I entreat you to set out immediately for Verona. […] I give you a thousand kisses.”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Roverbella, after the chase: beaten enemy, dead fatigue, Verona summoned. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have passed the whole night under arms. I should have taken Mantua by a bold and well directed blow, but the waters of the lake suddenly fell, and my columns, embarked, could not reach their landing-place. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Two hours after midnight at Marmirolo: a whole night under arms, Mantua missed. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “For two days I have had no letters from you. Thirty times to-day have I said this. You know therefore that I am very sad. You can not doubt the tender and absorbing solicitude with which you inspire me. We attacked Mantua yesterday. We bombarded it from two batteries with red-hot shot and shells. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Two days without her letters: thirty times counted in a day. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I hope that on arriving this evening, I shall receive one of your letters. You know, my dear Josephine, how much pleasure they give me. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Castiglione, 8 a.m.: hoping her letter arrives by evening. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The wants of the army require my presence in this region. It is impossible I should leave even to go to Milan. It would require five or six days. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: The army needs him: Milan must wait five or six days. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My first thought is to write to you. Your health and your image have not been out of my mind for one moment during the whole way. I shall not be happy until I have received letters from you. I wait for them with impatience. It is not possible that you can realize my distress. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Brescia: first thought on arrival is her. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We are in full campaign, my adorable friend. We have overthrown the outposts of the enemy. […] The troops are in fine spirits, and well disposed. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Ala, in full campaign: outposts overthrown. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I arrived at Verona day before yesterday, my dearest love. Though fatigued I am very well; much prospered, and I love you always passionately. I mount my horse. I embrace you a thousand times. BONAPARTE.”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Verona, day before yesterday arrived: fatigued, well, loving passionately. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I do not love you at all; on the contrary, I detest you. You are a naughty woman, very crooked, very unfeeling, very ungenerous. Tu es une vilaine, bien gauche, bien bête, bien cendrillon. You do not write me at all. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: The famous scolding: 'I do not love you at all' — Arcole-eve jealousy. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I hope very soon, my sweet love, to be in your arms. I love you most passionately. […] All goes well. Wurmser was beaten yesterday under Mantua. There is nothing wanted by your husband but the love of Josephine, in order to be happy.”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Wurmser beaten; loving 'à la fureur'. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received the express which Berthier had dispatched from Genoa. You had not time to write me. I feel it sensibly. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Milan, midnight: no letter — felt 'sensibly' amid gaiety. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).
